title: The Monk Who Inoculated the Ottoman Empire
event_summary: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of the British ambassador, witnessed Ottoman women practitioners performing variolation — the deliberate inoculation of smallpox matter into healthy patients — a technique perfected by Circassian folk healers and adopted across the empire. She had her own son inoculated by embassy surgeon Charles Maitland in Constantinople in March 1718, then campaigned ferociously to bring the practice to Britain. The technique she observed had been refined over generations by anonymous Ottoman and Circassian women healers whose names were never recorded, but whose method would become the direct precursor to Edward Jenner's vaccine seventy-eight years later.
why_forgotten: Western medical history credits Jenner's 1796 cowpox vaccine as the origin of immunization, largely erasing the Ottoman and Circassian folk tradition that preceded it by centuries. Montagu herself was dismissed by the male medical establishment of London, and the non-European origins of inoculation were downplayed to fit a narrative of European scientific supremacy. The anonymous Circassian and Turkish women who developed and transmitted the technique left no written records in European archives.
why_it_matters: This moment represents the critical bridge between ancient folk immunology and modern vaccination, the single most life-saving medical intervention in human history. Without Montagu's transfer of Ottoman knowledge, Britain's Royal Society experiments of the 1720s would never have occurred, and the intellectual groundwork for Jenner's later breakthrough might have been delayed by decades. The episode reveals that the entire global vaccination framework — from smallpox eradication to COVID-19 mRNA shots — traces its lineage not to a European laboratory but to unnamed women healers in the Muslim world.
